title: Span<T>: what does it improve and what constraints does it introduce?
description: Learn how Span<T> reduces allocations and copies in .NET, where it excels, and the safety constraints that come with ref-struct semantics.

data.text: `Span<T>` represents a contiguous region of arbitrary memory — an array, a stack-allocated buffer, or unmanaged memory — without copying it. Before `Span<T>`, many performance-critical methods needed separate overloads for arrays, `string`, `Memory<T>`, and pointers. `Span<T>` unifies these cases.

Because `Span<T>` is a `ref struct`, it lives on the stack and cannot be boxed, stored in fields, or captured by lambdas. This constraint is a safety feature: it guarantees the compiler will prevent you from escaping a slice beyond the lifetime of its backing store.

data.title: Performance gains
items: Parsing and formatting can read directly from source buffers without intermediate strings.
Slicing arrays or strings does not allocate a new array or substring object.
Interop and networking code can work with unmanaged memory safely.

data.content: This code extracts a date portion from a timestamp without creating intermediate strings.

data.title: Prefer ReadOnlySpan<T> when you do not write
data.text: `ReadOnlySpan<T>` communicates intent and allows the compiler to accept `string`, arrays, and `ReadOnlyMemory<T>` arguments without copying.

The `ref struct` constraint is the main trade-off. It keeps `Span<T>` safe but limits where you can use it. You cannot box it, store it in a class field, or use it across `await` boundaries because the stack frame may be gone when the method resumes.

rows: Use `Memory<T>` if you need heap storage
Length must be known or sliceable

data.text: When you need a `Span<T>`-like handle that can cross `await` or live in a class, use `Memory<T>`. `Memory<T>` can be created from the same sources as `Span<T>` but is a reference type. It copies less efficiently but is more flexible.

data.title: Span<T> vs Memory<T>
data.content: Choose Span<T> for synchronous, stack-confined algorithms. Choose Memory<T> when the handle must survive async boundaries.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Span<T> removes allocations for slicing, parsing, and copying contiguous memory.
ReadOnlySpan<T> is the safest default for read-only parameters.
ref struct constraints prevent boxing, heap storage, and await crossing.
Use Memory<T> when you need the same flexibility across async boundaries.
data.takeaway: Span<T> is a zero-cost abstraction over memory, but its safety constraints require matching your API design to its lifetime model.
